title: Act II, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: Calpurnia has dreamed of Caesar's statue spouting blood while Romans bathed their hands in it, and begs him to stay home. The augurs find no heart in a sacrificed beast. Caesar first boasts that danger knows he is more dangerous than it, then agrees to stay. Decius reinterprets the dream as Rome drawing life from Caesar, and says the Senate means to crown him and will mock him if he stays for a wife's dreams. Caesar goes; the conspirators and Antony arrive to escort him.

context.history: Augurs were Roman priests who read the will of the gods in sacrifices and the flight of birds.

significance: Caesar's pride and fear of looking weak are what Decius exploits, mirroring how Cassius worked on Brutus. Dramatic irony is strong: the audience knows the men greeting him as friends will kill him.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.
